analysis.one_liner: Dismantles VA-run veterans' health care and replaces it with subsidized private insurance plans.
analysis.headline: Referred to five House committees the day it was introduced, the bill to replace VA-run care with private insurance subsidies never got a hearing, markup, or vote and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have moved most VA health care out of government hands. It would have created a federally chartered nonprofit corporation, transferred VA hospitals, staff, and funds to it, and shut down the Veterans Health Administration's direct-care functions within about a year. Veterans would instead get subsidies to buy private insurance, on a sliding scale from full coverage for the most disabled veterans down to 60 percent of a plan's value for lower-priority veterans — while the lowest-priority new enrollees would get nothing.
analysis.who_benefits: Private health insurers gain a new, federally subsidized customer base: the bill pays premiums and cost-sharing for veterans in the VetsCare Choice program and pays Medicare premiums, cost-sharing, and Medigap premiums for Medicare-eligible veterans under VetsCare Senior. Private hospitals and physicians gain newly insured veteran patients. Some veterans gain too: those who live far from VA facilities or prefer private providers get subsidized choice, the most disabled veterans get full-coverage support, and Medicare-eligible veterans get their Medicare premiums and cost-sharing paid in full.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Private insurers; veterans wanting private care

how_it_helps.text: Creates the Veterans Accountable Care Organization, a federally chartered nonprofit, and transfers all VA personnel, property, and funds used for direct care to it; the Veterans Health Administration's direct-care functions terminate one year after enactment, with up to two 90-day extensions.

Establishes premium support for private insurance in tiers: 100 percent of a plan's value for veterans rated 100 percent disabled, 90 percent for priority groups 1-2, 80 percent for groups 3-4, 70 percent for groups 5-6, and 60 percent for everyone else eligible — with the subsidy pegged to the second-cheapest plan in the veteran's area.
Pays Medicare premiums and cost-sharing under Parts A, B, C, and D, plus Medigap supplemental premiums, in full for Medicare-eligible veterans in the VetsCare Senior program.

Adds low-income protections — extra premium and cost-sharing help for veterans under roughly 400 percent of the poverty line — lets veterans put support into health savings accounts, and preserves access to VA pharmacies for enrollees.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the new premium-support and Medicare-payment obligations. Veterans bear the difference: most get subsidies covering only 60 to 90 percent of a plan's value, pegged to the second-cheapest plan, so they pay the remaining premiums, deductibles, and copays that VA care today largely does not charge. Veterans newly enrolling in priority groups 7 or 8 would be excluded from insurance support entirely. VA health care workers face transfer to the new corporation or a reduction in force.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and veterans paying new premiums

drawbacks.text: The bill replaces direct VA care — which charges most veterans no premiums and modest copays — with capped subsidies, so most veterans would take on premiums, deductibles, and copays out of pocket, and new enrollees in priority groups 7-8 would get no support at all.

It requires the Veterans Health Administration's direct-care functions to terminate within about a year (extendable by at most two 90-day periods), an extremely short window to move a hospital system with hundreds of thousands of employees into a new corporation without disrupting care.

The bill sets up large new premium-support obligations without a dedicated funding source — the fund it creates covers only centers of excellence and care at corporation facilities — leaving the cost of subsidizing millions of veterans' insurance unspecified.

It makes private insurers the permanent channel for veterans' coverage, with the subsidy benchmarked to the second-cheapest plan, meaning the value of veterans' benefits would depend on local private-market prices rather than a guaranteed government benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are real but unevenly spread: Medicare-eligible veterans and the most severely disabled would do well, and veterans far from VA facilities would gain options. But for most veterans the trade is worse — a free or low-cost direct care system swapped for capped subsidies covering 60 to 90 percent of a private plan's value, with the lowest-priority new enrollees excluded entirely and a one-year deadline to dissolve direct care. The design shifts costs onto veterans and locks insurers in as middlemen, and the bill offers no funding mechanism for the new obligations. On balance, this was a privatization bill whose costs would have fallen mainly on the veterans it named in its title.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to five different House committees the day it was introduced, got no hearing or vote in any of them, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Doug Lamborn introduced the bill on November 21, 2017, joined by Reps. Mark Meadows and Trent Franks as original cosponsors; four Republicans cosponsored in total.

That same day, the House referred it to five committees — Veterans' Affairs, Ways and Means, Oversight and Government Reform, Energy and Commerce, and Armed Services — splitting it among jurisdictions with no single committee in charge.

It was then assigned to the Veterans' Affairs Subcommittee on Health and the Armed Services Subcommittee on Military Personnel, where it sat with no hearings, markups, or votes for the rest of the 115th Congress.
The bill died on January 3, 2019, when the 115th Congress ended and all unpassed legislation expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Veterans who rely on the VA's direct care system — free or low-cost care without premiums — keep it, because the bill never advanced. Private insurers do not gain the new federally subsidized veteran market the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Veterans relying on direct VA care

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on the bill; the sponsor and all four cosponsors were House Republicans, and no Democrat publicly supported it.

industries.note: The bill would pay insurers premiums and cost-sharing for veterans in VetsCare Choice and would cover Medicare and Medigap premiums in full for Medicare-eligible veterans, making private plans the permanent channel for veterans' coverage. Their gain comes from replacing a cheaper public alternative — direct VA care with no premiums — with capped subsidies that leave veterans paying the difference.

Millions of veterans with new federal insurance subsidies would seek care in the private sector, and the new corporation's facilities could even contract as designated providers under private plans. Veterans gain choice, but the mechanism ends the public system that delivered that care directly.

industries.industry: Veterans Health Administration (VA hospitals and staff)
industries.note: The bill terminates the VHA's direct-care functions within about a year and transfers its personnel, property, and funds to a new federally chartered corporation, authorizing a reduction in force. What the VHA loses is exactly the direct, low-cost access veterans would lose with it.
